{{Short description|Informal fallacy}}
{{One source|date=November 2025}}
{{Italic title}}
'''''Secundum quid''''' (comes from the Latin "a dicto simpliciter ad dictum secundum quid", meaning "[what is true] in a certain respect and [what is true] absolutely" or "from the statement unqualified to the statement qualified).<ref>{{Cite web |title=a dicto simpliciter ad dictum secundum quid |url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803095717416 |access-date=August 7, 2026 |website=Oxford Reference}}</ref>
It is a type of informal fallacy that occurs when the arguer omits the fact that a statement applies with qualifications or exceptions, or fails to recognize the difference between [[rules of thumb]] (''soft'' generalizations, [[heuristics]] that hold true ''as a general rule'' but leave room for exceptions) and [[categorical proposition]]s, rules that hold true universally.

Since it ignores the limits, or [[wikt:qualification|qualifications]], of rules of thumb, this fallacy is also named '''ignoring qualifications''' or '''sweeping generalizations'''. The expression '''misuse of a principle''' can be used as well.<ref name="Damer2009" />

==Example==
{{quote|Let me tell you: all great composers die young. Take Mendelssohn: he was 38. Or Mozart, just 35. And Schubert! Hundreds of songs, and he was only 31.}}
The arguer cites only the cases that support his point, conveniently omitting Bach, Beethoven, Brahms etc

==In popular culture==
The following quatrain can be attributed to C. H. Talbot:

{{Poem quote|
I talked in terms whose sense was hid,
''[[Fallacy of division|Dividendo]], [[Fallacy of composition|componendo]] et secundum quid'';
Now ''secundum quid'' is a wise remark
And it earned my reputation as a learned clerk.}}

==2 Types==
{{Expand section|date=October 2014}}
Instances of ''secundum quid'' are of two kinds:
* [[Accident (fallacy)|Accident]] — ''a dicto simpliciter ad dictum secundum quid'' (where an acceptable exception is ignored) [from general to qualified]. This is taking the usual case and inappropriately applying it to special cases. This is when we can't or don't want to list the exceptions to a reasoning, and then use it as a generalization as if there was no exception.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fallacies {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/ |access-date=2026-08-07 |language=en-US}}</ref>
* [[Converse accident]] — ''a dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter'' (where an acceptable exception is eliminated or simplified) [from qualified to general]. This is taking one unusual case and inappropriately applying it to all cases. This is when we focus on one exception and use it to draw a generalization. It is close to [[hasty generalization]]. <ref>{{Cite web |title=Fallacies {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/ |access-date=2026-08-07 |language=en-US}}</ref>
